newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers vow to crack down on tax breaks.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers vow to crack down on tax breaks.

text.p: European Union finance ministers vowed on Monday to crack down on tax breaks which they said could create unfair competition among countries sharing a single market and soon to share a single currency.
"We are going to go after tax oases energetically," German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told reporters at a finance ministers' meeting.
"We believe in tax competition but it must be a fair competition. We need common rules of play."

The surprise announcement by different ministers that they wanted to try to reduce big disparities in taxes across the bloc revived an idea, which, though considered informally for years, has never really got off the ground.
"This is a subject which has been neglected for too long," Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said in a televised speech at the start of the talks.

Europe's plans to launch a single currency in less than two years' time -- on January 1, 1999 -- appear to have refocused attention on an issue long dogged by fears of ceding national sovereignty over taxation to European institutions.
"It is due to the monetary union plans," Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt told reporters.
The launch of the euro would make it all the more unacceptable that companies and savers were shifting investments around Europe to cash in on the best tax regime, he said.

Luxembourg is a particular problem for its neighbours, having built a thriving private banking centre by attracting vast numbers of Belgian and other savers drawn to the tax advantages of being a non-resident investor.
Maystadt said the main focus of European efforts to reduce tax differences should be on company taxes and savings taxes.
Ministers and officials were quick to stress there was no question of Europe trying to impose income tax levels on national governments.
"There is no legal basis to deal with income tax," European Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy said.
"It does not involve a central European tax system as some people think," Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm told Reuters Financial Television, adding the aim was rather to crack down on tax evasion.
Ministers however seemed a long way from working out how they would go about reducing disparities in taxation, or even in defining what constituted unfair competition.
Waigel, when asked the difference between fair and unfair competition, answered simply, "the word 'un.'"
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told reporters he would like to seek rules of good conduct to discourage EU members from competing unfairly with each other.

Another possibility, Maystadt said, would be to end the distinction between resident and non-resident status for EU citizens, which allows them to escape paying tax at source on savings placed in another EU country.
In theory those investing abroad are meant to declare investment income in their own country, but many do not.
The tax talks briefly overshadowed another debate currently simmering in Europe -- over a French proposal for a euro-zone stability council to co-ordinate economic policies after 1999.
Officials had said the idea, attacked by the Bundesbank as a potential threat to the independence of the future European Central Bank (ECB), might be raised informally at the talks.
But Arthuis and other ministers said the matter had not been raised. He insisted there was no row over his proposal and repeated that France favoured an independent central bank
The proposal was gaining favour among France's EU partners, and "there is no dispute," he said.
